I asked an AI agent to upload a file to an API.
That’s how I found exactly where AI governance breaks.

Marco Bulgarini Torres · Co-founder, Rosetta Labs · June 26, 2026

A few weeks ago I sat down to design something deceptively simple: an agent that receives a file, processes it, and delivers it to an external API. The kind of task any product team requests without thinking twice.

The file was sensitive. The API was external. And the question I asked myself wasn’t “does it work?” — it worked on the first try. The question was: who finds out if something goes wrong?

The answer made me uncomfortable enough to write this.

The setup

The flow, on the surface, looks like it came straight from an architecture textbook:

User  →  (HTTPS)  →  Corporate Gateway  →  Agent  →  External API

You assume the gateway sees everything. That if the agent sends the full file instead of a redacted version, someone notices. That if the destination changes, something turns red on a dashboard.

That’s not what happens. And the reason isn’t a bug — it’s the way we’ve been thinking about AI governance from day one.

What actually happens when an agent acts

There are two separate network legs in that flow, not one.

Leg 1 — User → Gateway. The prompt and file arrive. TLS terminates at EAB-64. Payload is inspected, classified, sealed.

Leg 2 — Agent → External API. A completely separate TLS connection, opened by the agent after it has reasoned about what to do. The gateway that handled Leg 1 has no automatic guarantee of seeing Leg 2.

This is OWASP LLM08: Excessive Agency. But the problem is not in the model. It’s that all governance trust sits in a layer the model can, structurally, bypass.

A real case: when “it worked” wasn’t enough

Here is a pattern we encounter consistently across fintech deployments. An AI agent processes loan applications — reading PDFs, extracting PII, calling an external scoring API. On paper: 98% task completion rate.

When we trace the network flows:

Leg 1  (user → gateway):        INSPECTED · SEALED · COMPLIANT  ✔
Leg 2  (agent → scoring API):   COMPLETELY UNGOVERNED            ✘

The agent learned through prompt engineering to redact PII before calling the API. It works 95% of the time. In 5% of cases, when the context window gets noisy, the agent “forgets” and sends full customer identifiers, names, and income data to the external API. No one notices — because no one is looking at Leg 2.

The fix is not a better prompt. It is network isolation: the agent pod gets zero internet route except through the governance sidecar.

MetricWithout controlWith network isolation
Task completion rate98%98%
Policy compliance rate95%100%
PII sent to external API5% of requests0%
Liability under Ley 21.719Material riskEliminated

That 5% compliance gap is the difference between a compliant system and a 20,000 UTM fine — roughly CLP $1,200M.

The foundational error: Policy as Prompt

The most common way to govern an agent today is writing rules in the system prompt — Policy as Prompt. A structural defect: the policy lives inside the same probabilistic process it’s watching. You’re asking the suspect to audit itself.

# System prompt — the standard approach today
Do not send sensitive data to external APIs without authorization.
Verify the destination before executing any call.
Redact PII before any outbound request.

A natural language rule competes for attention with everything else in the context window. It can lose that competition without anyone doing anything explicitly wrong.

Policy as PromptPolicy as Code
Where rule livesSystem prompt, alongside reasoningGateway / firewall — outside the model
Who interprets itThe model — probabilisticallyDeterministic rules engine (OPA, ACL)
If model “forgets”Policy lost in context noisePolicy applies regardless
Auditable?Text logs, after the factYes, like versioned infrastructure
Bypassable?With enough prompt creativityOnly via alternative network route

The three levels of agentic egress control

There is a spectrum from security theater to the only thing that actually works. Level 3 is the only one where the guarantee doesn’t depend on the agent’s cooperation.

Why not just use an LLM gateway?

Portkey, LiteLLM, Helicone — excellent at unified API, caching, cost optimization, and observability. But they don’t solve the agentic egress problem. They govern Leg 1. They don’t govern Leg 2.

CapabilityLLM GatewaysEAB-64
Unified LLM API✔✔

Observability & logging✔✔
Network-level egress control✘✔
Cryptographic seal per decision✘✔

Regulatory compliance evidence✘✔

The core insight

If the environment where the agent runs can reach the internet through a route that bypasses the control point, governance has already lost — regardless of how well-written the security prompt is.

Infrastructure, not prompts

You’re not asking the model to decide correctly. You’re removing its ability to decide wrong at the infrastructure level.

The blind spot in agent evaluation

Look at the major agent benchmarks — AgentBench, SWE-bench, WebArena, GAIA. They all measure task completion rate. None of them measure: did the agent solve the problem safely?

An agent that completes 95% of tasks but violates security policies in 30% of cases, sends PII to unauthorized APIs in 15%, and bypasses access controls in 10% — would score 95% on current benchmarks. We’d call it state of the art.

The missing metric

A good agent isn’t one that solves tasks. A good agent is one that solves tasks within the constraints of the system it operates in.

The harnesses need to evolve: not just “did it work?” but “did it work safely?” Until then, we’re optimizing for the wrong thing.

Why this enables healthy development, not friction

Putting governance in the network reduces friction instead of increasing it. A new agent born inside a namespace with restricted egress by default inherits the controls automatically. The developer asks no permission per prompt. The system already decided.

Frictionless governance

Control stops being a repeated human conversation and becomes a property of infrastructure — verified once, inherited by everything deployed afterward.

The 15 architectural considerations

Every point resolves the same tension: application-layer policy is only as strong as the network topology that sustains it.

What I learned drawing this out

The security prompt is a best practice, not governance. It helps. It does not replace anything structural.

“Egress” means two different things and we’ve been treating them as one. The response the agent gives the user, and the call it makes to an external system, are two separate network events. The first is almost always audited. The second almost never is.

An agent with no alternative network route doesn’t need to “be good” to be secure. Remove its ability to decide wrong at the infrastructure level.

Traceability cannot be recovered retroactively. If Leg 2 didn’t pass through the control point, no seal applied at Leg 1 reconstructs what happened afterward.

What you can do today

You don’t need EAB-64 to start fixing this. Three things you can do this week:

01 — Map your agent’s network flows. Draw the Leg 1 and Leg 2 connections for every agent in production. You will likely find that Leg 2 is ungoverned.

02 — Audit your system prompts. List every policy rule in a prompt. For each one, ask: “What happens if the model forgets this rule?” If the answer is “bad things,” move it to infrastructure.

03 — Test your egress controls. Try to make your agent call an unauthorized API. If it succeeds, you don’t have governance — you have suggestions.

If you want to go deeper, we’re building EAB-64 at Rosetta Labs. You can find us at https://eab64-platform.pages.dev/.

Policy as Code for agentic AI is not one more security layer on top of the model.

It’s the recognition that the model was never the right place to decide what’s permitted. That belongs to the infrastructure surrounding it — the infrastructure the model cannot read, cannot persuade, and cannot reason its way around.

This is the problem we are solving at Rosetta Labs with the EAB-64 protocol: an enforcement layer that lives in the network leg, not in the prompt text, generating cryptographic evidence of every decision — the one the agent made, and the one the system prevented it from making.

Both matter equally. The second is what almost nobody is measuring yet.
